body.statement: Let \(t_{\mathrm{bal}}\) solve \(t=\{\phi(t)+t\Phi(t)\}/2\) and let \(\kappa_{\mathrm{bal}}=\Phi(t_{\mathrm{bal}})/2=0.3043687064\ldots\). Then \(\mathbb P(\mathcal E_{0n}\cap\mathcal E_{1n}\cap\mathcal Q_n)\to1\) when \(\kappa<\kappa_{\mathrm{bal}}\), while \(\mathbb P(\mathcal E_{0n}\cap\mathcal E_{1n})\to0\) when \(\kappa>\kappa_{\mathrm{bal}}\). In the interior regime, \(\mathcal E_{0n}\cap\mathcal E_{1n}\cap\mathcal Q_n\) is therefore the certified event on which both arms use their unique exact-balancing entropy solutions and the ordinary full-rank leverage identities apply.
body.justification: The theorem identifies the exact domain on which proportional exact entropy balancing exists.
body.gap: ZhaoPercival2017 gives fixed-dimensional interiority and DaiYan2024 documents high-dimensional infeasibility; neither derives the endogenous pooled-target threshold.
body.consumer: The threshold tells trial analysts when exact same-coordinate balancing is mathematically unavailable before any policy comparison is attempted.
body.proof_tex:
Fix an arm \(a\), condition on its index set \(I_{an}=\{i:A_{ni}=a\}\), and write \(m=|I_{an}|\) and \(\alpha_m=m/n\).  The exceptional cases \(m\in\{0,n\}\) have probability tending to zero under randomization.  For one feature coordinate, the vector of centered arm rows
\[
 C^{(\ell)}=(q_{ni,\ell}-\bar q_{n,\ell}:i\in I_{an})^{\top}
\]
is centered Gaussian and has covariance
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}(C^{(\ell)}_i,C^{(\ell)}_k)
 =\mathbf 1\{i=k\}-\frac1n.
\]
Different feature coordinates remain independent.  With \(u=m^{-1/2}\mathbf 1_m\), define
\[
 \Sigma_m=I_m-\alpha_m uu^{\top},\qquad
 A_m=\Sigma_m^{1/2}=I_m-c_muu^{\top},\qquad
 c_m=1-\sqrt{1-\alpha_m}.
\]
Because \(0<\alpha_m<1\), \(A_m\) is invertible.  The centered arm matrix \(C_m\) therefore has the distribution
\[
 C_m=A_mG_m,qquad G_m\in\mathbb R^{m\times p_n}
 \text{ with independent }\mathcal N(0,1)\text{ entries}.
\]

A finite convex combination represents \(\bar q_n\) as a relative-interior point of the arm hull if and only if it can be represented with every coefficient strictly positive.  Indeed, every strictly positive combination is in the relative interior.  Conversely, average all arm points to obtain a relative-interior point \(z\); if \(y\) is in the relative interior, then for sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\), \(y'=(y-\varepsilon z)/(1-\varepsilon)\) remains in the hull, and \(y=(1-\varepsilon)y'+\varepsilon z\) has a representation with all coefficients positive.  Applying this equivalence to \(y=\bar q_n\) shows that
\[
 \mathcal E_{an}quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \ker(G_m^{\top})\cap\operatorname{int}(K_m)\ne\varnothing,
 \qquad K_m=A_m\mathbb R_+^m,
\]
apart from the already excluded empty-arm case.  The nullspace of the independent Gaussian matrix is Haar distributed on the Grassmannian.  To compare interior and closed-cone intersection, put \(B_m=G_m^{\top}A_m\).  Almost surely, simultaneously for every column set \(I\), the submatrix \((B_m)_I\) has rank \(\min(p_n,|I|)\): each such submatrix has a nonsingular Gaussian row covariance because every principal submatrix of \(A_m^2=\Sigma_m\) is positive definite, and there are only finitely many \(I\).  Suppose \(B_mw=0\) for a nonzero \(w\ge0\), and let \(I=\{i:w_i>0\}\).  Full column rank rules out \(|I|\le p_n\), so \(|I|>p_n\) and \((B_m)_I\) has full row rank.  For each \(j\notin I\), choose \(v^{(j)}_I\) solving \((B_m)_Iv^{(j)}_I=-(B_m)_j\), put \(v^{(j)}_j=1\), and put its other coordinates outside \(I\) equal to zero.  Then \(B_mv^{(j)}=0\).  Choosing all positive coefficients \(\varepsilon_j\) sufficiently small makes
\[
 w'=w+\sum_{j\notin I}\varepsilon_jv^{(j)}
\]
strictly positive while preserving \(B_mw'=0\).  Thus closed-cone intersection implies interior intersection almost surely; the converse is immediate.  Hence the last event agrees almost surely with
\[
 \ker(G_m^{\top})\cap K_m\ne\{0\}.
\]

We next calculate the statistical dimension of \(K_m\).  Let \(G=(G_1,\ldots,G_m)^{\top}\sim\mathcal N(0,I_m)\).  By the cited metric characterization, projection onto \(K_m\) is obtained by minimizing \(\|G-A_mw\|_2^2\) over \(w\ge0\).  Since \(A_m^{\top}A_m=\Sigma_m\), the coordinate Karush--Kuhn--Tucker conditions, which are sufficient because this quadratic is strictly convex, are
\[
 w_i=\bigl(G_i-c_m\bar G+t_m\bigr)_+,qquad
 t_m=\alpha_m\overline w
     =\alpha_m\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m
       \bigl(G_i-c_m\bar G+t_m\bigr)_+.
\]
The right side of the scalar fixed-point equation is Lipschitz in \(t_m\) with constant at most \(\alpha_m<1\), so the solution is unique.  If \(\alpha_m\to\alpha\in(0,1)\), the law of large numbers, \(\bar G\to0\), and the contraction bound imply
\[
 t_m\longrightarrow t_\alpha,qquad
 t_\alpha=\alpha H(t_\alpha),qquad
 H(t)=\mathbb E(G_1+t)_+=\phi(t)+t\Phi(t).
\]
The root is unique and positive because the derivative of \(\alpha H(t)-t\) is \(\alpha\Phi(t)-1<0\), its value at zero is \(\alpha\phi(0)>0\), and it tends to minus infinity as \(t\to\infty\).

For the minimizing \(w\),
\[
 \frac1m\|\Pi_{K_m}(G)\|_2^2
 =\frac1m w^{\top}\Sigma_mw
 =\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^mw_i^2-\alpha_m\overline w^{,2}.
\]
The same law-of-large-numbers argument gives convergence in probability of the right side to
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E(G_1+t_\alpha)_+^2-\alpha H(t_\alpha)^2
 &=(1+t_\alpha^2)\Phi(t_\alpha)+t_\alpha\phi(t_\alpha)
   -t_\alpha H(t_\alpha)\\
 &=\Phi(t_\alpha),
 \end{aligned}
\]
where the fixed-point equation was used in the first line.  Projection contraction gives \(\|\Pi_{K_m}(G)\|_2^2/m\le\|G\|_2^2/m\), and \(\mathbb E(\|G\|_2^2/m)^2=1+2/m\).  Uniform integrability and the cited metric characterization therefore yield
\[
 \frac{\delta(K_m)}m\longrightarrow\Phi(t_\alpha).
\]

Assume now that \(p_n/m\to\kappa/\alpha\).  A fixed subspace of dimension \(m-p_n\) has statistical dimension \(m-p_n\), because the expected squared norm of the projection of a standard Gaussian vector onto it is \(m-p_n\).  Thus
\[
 \delta(K_m)+(m-p_n)-m
 =m\left\{\Phi(t_\alpha)-\frac\kappa\alpha\right\}+o(m).
\]
For any fixed separation from \(\kappa=\alpha\Phi(t_\alpha)\), this quantity has magnitude of order \(m\), and hence eventually dominates the \(a_\eta\sqrt m\) transition width in the cited approximate kinematic formula.  Letting the fixed tolerance \(\eta\downarrow0\) proves conditional feasibility probability tending to one below \(\alpha\Phi(t_\alpha)\), and tending to zero above it.

By Chebyshev's inequality applied to the independent treatment indicators, \(n_{an}/n\to1/2\) in probability for both arms.  The preceding deterministic-sequence argument is uniform over counts in a sufficiently small neighborhood of \(n/2\): otherwise a countersequence of counts would contradict the proved limit.  Removing the conditioning and using a union bound consequently gives
\[
 \mathbb P(\mathcal E_{0n}\cap\mathcal E_{1n})\to1
 \quad\text{if }\kappa<\tfrac12\Phi(t_{1/2}),
\]
and in fact \(\mathbb P(\mathcal E_{0n}\cup\mathcal E_{1n})\to0\) if \(\kappa>\tfrac12\Phi(t_{1/2})\).  Since \(\kappa<1/2\), eventually \(p_n<n\); the Gaussian matrix \(Q_n\) then has column rank \(p_n\) almost surely, so adjoining \(\mathcal Q_n\) does not alter the first limit.

Finally, when \(\alpha=1/2\), the scalar equation is exactly
\[
 t_{\mathrm{bal}}=\{\phi(t_{\mathrm{bal}})+t_{\mathrm{bal}}\Phi(t_{\mathrm{bal}})\}/2,
 \qquad \kappa_{\mathrm{bal}}=\Phi(t_{\mathrm{bal}})/2.
\]
Monotonicity already proves uniqueness.  Direct interval evaluation gives
\(0.2760298047<t_{\mathrm{bal}}<0.2760298049\) and
\(0.304368706413<\Phi(t_{\mathrm{bal}})/2<0.304368706453\), which establishes the displayed decimal.  On the joint event, extend \(w\log(n_{an}w)\) continuously by zero at \(w=0\).  The feasible simplex is compact, so a minimizer exists, and strict convexity makes it unique.  If this minimizer had a zero coordinate, moving toward the strictly positive feasible vector established above would have directional derivative minus infinity because \(t\log t\) has that derivative at zero; this contradicts minimality.  The minimizer is therefore strictly positive, the equality-constrained Lagrange equations give the exponential-tilt form, and the stipulated minimum-norm rule resolves any dual nonidentifiability.  Thus both arms use their unique exact-balancing entropy solutions.  Finally, \(\mathcal Q_n\) gives the ordinary inverse formula for the full-sample resolvent.
